Synthetic rainfall

Source: R/synthetic_rain.R
synthetic_rain.Rd

Generates a regular series of rain and potential evaporation, mm per step, for driving a model. Four rainfall generators are available:

Usage

synthetic_rain(
  start,
  years = 10,
  dt = 1,
  method = c("nsrp", "bartlett_lewis", "markov_gamma", "resample"),
  parameters = NULL,
  record = NULL,
  pet = list(mean = 1.5, amplitude = 1.3, peak_day = 182),
  block_days = 10,
  window_days = 15,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

start

First time, as text or POSIXct (UTC).

years

Length in years (365 days each).

dt

Step, hours: 0.25, 1, 24 or any value that divides a day or is a whole number of days.

method

Generator; see the table.

parameters

A parameter table from rain_parameters() or fit_rain().

record

A rainfall record to fit or resample: a data frame with time (or dateTime) and rain (or value, mm per step), or an object from reach.io::read_silver().

pet

List of mean (mm per day), amplitude (mm per day) and peak_day (day of the year), or NULL for no PET column.

block_days, window_days

For resample: block length and how far, in days, from the same date a block may be drawn.

seed

Optional seed; the caller's random state is left untouched.

Value

A data frame with time (POSIXct, UTC), rain and, unless pet = NULL, pet, both mm per step, ready for run_pdm() or synthetic_catchment(). Attributes record the method and the parameters used.

Details

  • nsrp (default): Neyman-Scott rectangular pulses. Storms arrive at random, each spawning a random number of rain cells, delayed from the storm's origin, each with its own duration and intensity (Cowpertwait 1996). Widely used for UK rainfall. Any step.

  • bartlett_lewis: Bartlett-Lewis rectangular pulses. As above, but a storm produces cells at a steady rate until it stops (Rodriguez-Iturbe et al. 1987; the original model, with a fixed cell duration rate). Any step.

  • markov_gamma: wet and dry days from a two-state Markov chain, wet-day amounts from a gamma distribution (Richardson 1981). Daily only.

  • resample: a seasonal block bootstrap of a real record: blocks of whole days drawn from any year within a few weeks of the same date. The rain is real; the sequence is new. It cannot produce a storm bigger than the record holds. The record's step, or a multiple.

Parameters vary by calendar month. Without parameters or record, the built-in illustrative values of rain_parameters() are used. With record, the generator is first fitted to it by fit_rain() (for resample, the record is used directly).

PET follows a sine curve through the year (as reach.io's generate_pe_sine() does), peaking at pet$peak_day, and is spread evenly over the steps of each day. It is never negative.

References

Cowpertwait, P.S.P. (1996) Further developments of the Neyman-Scott clustered point process for modeling rainfall. Water Resources Research 32(7), 2155-2164.

Rodriguez-Iturbe, I., Cox, D.R. and Isham, V. (1987) Some models for rainfall based on stochastic point processes. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A 410, 269-288.

Richardson, C.W. (1981) Stochastic simulation of daily precipitation, temperature, and solar radiation. Water Resources Research 17(1), 182-190.

See also

fit_rain(), rain_parameters(), synthetic_catchment()

Examples

hourly <- synthetic_rain("2020-10-01", years = 1, seed = 1)
sum(hourly$rain)
#> [1] 841.8127
daily <- synthetic_rain("2020-10-01", years = 2, dt = 24, method = "markov_gamma", seed = 1)
head(daily)
#>         time     rain      pet
#> 1 2020-10-01 7.327184 1.462267
#> 2 2020-10-02 2.397931 1.439920
#> 3 2020-10-03 0.000000 1.417591
#> 4 2020-10-04 0.000000 1.395286
#> 5 2020-10-05 4.307307 1.373012
#> 6 2020-10-06 0.000000 1.350776
